name: Calla Winterbourne
line: Runs a one-person boatyard and restores old wooden sailboats for private clients.

project.title: Sparrowhawk
project.logline: A 1950s 22-foot wooden sloop being rebuilt for a client's spring launch.
constraints: Keep the original lines: no fibreglass sheathing over the hull planks.
The client launches on the last Saturday of April, so the hull must be tight by mid-April.
The budget is fixed, so salvaged bronze fittings are used wherever they are sound.

statements.text: They are rebuilding the Sparrowhawk, a 22-foot wooden sloop, for a client's spring launch.
They prefer steam-bent oak ribs over laminated ones when the original used solid timber.
They would rather close a seam with cotton and linseed putty than with a modern sealant.
They like working notes as short numbered steps, not paragraphs.
They want blunt answers with no reassurance.
They want the answer first and the reasons after it.

preferences.text: They distrust quick-fix filler and want a proper scarf joint wherever a plank is damaged.
They would take a simpler rig that needs no adjusting under way over a clever one.
They want a written cut list before any timber is cut.

new_work: The client now wants a small inboard engine fitted in the Sparrowhawk. I have to lay out an engine bed that carries the load without stressing the keel bolts. How would you set it up?
One plank just above the waterline has a hairline split along the grain, and the client says to run epoxy into it and paint over. What should I do about that plank?
I found the original rudder fittings in a salvage lot: bronze, pitted, but not cracked. How do I decide whether to clean and reuse them or have new ones cast?
